Write-Ahead Logging in SQLite

By Sam Rivera · March 3, 2026

SQLite ships with two journaling strategies. The default rollback journal copies original pages aside before changing the database file, while write-ahead logging appends changes to a separate WAL file and leaves the database untouched until a checkpoint. This article walks through why WAL mode usually wins for applications with concurrent readers.

How the rollback journal works

In rollback mode a writer first copies every page it will modify into the journal file. Only then does it overwrite the pages in the main database. If the process crashes halfway through, the next connection notices the hot journal and restores the original pages, so the database is never left half-written.

The cost is that a writer needs an exclusive lock on the whole database while it commits. Readers are blocked for the duration of every write transaction, which hurts latency on busy web servers.

How WAL mode works

With write-ahead logging, commits append new versions of pages to the WAL file. Readers keep seeing a consistent snapshot by consulting the WAL index, a shared-memory structure that maps page numbers to their latest committed frame. Writers never block readers and readers never block writers.

Checkpoints

Periodically SQLite runs a checkpoint that copies committed frames from the WAL back into the main database file. By default this happens automatically once the WAL reaches 1000 pages. A checkpoint cannot complete past a frame that an active reader still needs, so very long read transactions can make the WAL grow without bound.

Comparing the modes

PropertyRollback journalWAL
Readers during a writeBlockedAllowed
Files on diskdb + journaldb + wal + shm
Network filesystemsSupportedNot supported
Write throughputLowerHigher

Enabling WAL

WAL mode is persistent: once a database is switched, every later connection uses it. You enable it with a single pragma and should also set a busy timeout so writers wait instead of failing immediately.

import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
conn.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000")
conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")

Remember that foreign key enforcement is a per-connection setting and must be enabled every time a connection is opened, unlike the journal mode.
